nameStory: Parlin's pussytoes gets its charming name from the soft, fuzzy flower heads that feel just like a kitten's paw pad when you gently touch them. The 'Parlin's' part honors John Crawford Parlin, a botanist who worked at the University of Maine in the early 1900s and helped document many of New England's wild plants. Like all pussytoes, this plant's scientific name Antennaria comes from the Latin word for antenna, referring to the feathery bristles on the seeds that help them float away on the wind.
description: Parlin's pussytoes is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms spreading mats close to the ground. The plant reaches only 4-12 inches tall, with small clusters of white to pinkish fuzzy flower heads that bloom in spring and early summer. Its leaves are spoon-shaped and covered in soft, woolly hairs that give them a grayish-green appearance. This plant spreads by underground runners, creating patches that can persist for many years in the same spot.

habitat: Parlin's pussytoes thrives in dry, open areas with well-drained soils throughout New England. Look for it in sunny meadows, old fields, sandy or rocky slopes, and along woodland edges where the soil isn't too rich or moist. It's particularly fond of disturbed areas and can often be found growing in thin soils where other plants struggle.

seasonality.spring: Fuzzy white to pink flower clusters appear in late spring, typically May through early June, rising above the mat of woolly leaves.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and are replaced by fluffy white seed heads that disperse in the wind by mid to late summer. Leaves remain green and woolly.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may take on reddish tints but often stay somewhat green through the season, forming low mats that persist.
seasonality.winter: Basal rosettes of woolly leaves often remain visible through winter, especially in milder areas, looking like small silvery-gray cushions against the snow.

funFact: Parlin's pussytoes is what botanists call 'dioecious,' meaning individual plants are either all-male or all-female - you'll never find both types of flowers on the same plant! The female plants produce the fluffy seed heads we see blowing in the wind, while male plants have smaller, less showy flowers.
confusionNotes: Parlin's pussytoes can be tricky to distinguish from other pussytoes species without close examination, but it's generally larger and more robust than Small Pussytoes and has more rounded leaves than the narrow-leaved Field Pussytoes. Memory trick: if the fuzzy flowers feel like kitten paws and the plant forms spreading mats in dry, open areas, you're likely looking at a pussytoes species.
contextualKnowledge: The pussytoes genus can be challenging for beginners because several species look very similar and often hybridize with each other in the wild. Don't worry about getting the exact species right at first - just enjoy recognizing the distinctive 'kitten paw' flowers that make all pussytoes special.
compareHints: Parlin's pussytoes is generally more robust and taller than Small Pussytoes, and has broader, more spoon-shaped leaves compared to the narrower leaves of Field Pussytoes. Unlike Plantain-leaved Pussytoes, which has distinctly ribbed leaves, Parlin's has smooth-edged spoon-shaped leaves. All pussytoes share that characteristic soft, woolly texture and fuzzy flower heads, but Parlin's tends to form the most extensive spreading mats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Small Pussytoes lives up to its name by being noticeably smaller than its relatives - its leaves are typically under 2 inches long compared to Field Pussytoes which can have 4-inch leaves.
Field pussytoes differs from small pussytoes by being taller and having more flower heads per cluster.

Among the pussytoes species in New England, plantain-leaved pussytoes is distinguished by its notably broader, more prominently veined leaves compared to field pussytoes or small pussytoes, which have much narrower, less obviously ribbed foliage.
Catsfoot differs from other New England pussytoes by its preference for cooler, mountainous habitats and its particularly silvery-white, woolly appearance.
